claim: Programmed cell death fine-tunes the density of neuronal populations by eliminating 20–40% of overproduced neurons.
source: In the nervous system, programmed cell death (PCD) fine-tunes the density of neuronal populations by eliminating 20–40% of overproduced neurons (Fuchs and Steller, 2011; Causeret et al., 2018; Wong and Marín, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fuchs and Steller, 2011; Causeret et al., 2018; Wong and Marín, 2019

claim: Only few populations of the mouse cerebral cortex almost completely disappear during the first two postnatal weeks.
source: Only few populations of the mouse cerebral cortex almost completely disappear during the first two postnatal weeks.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: Cajal-Retzius cells undergo extensive cell death in the mouse during the second postnatal week.
source: Amongst these, Cajal-Retzius cells (CRs), the first-born cortical neurons lying in the superficial Layer I (LI), undergo extensive cell death in the mouse during the second postnatal week (Ledonne et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ledonne et al., 2016

claim: The persistence of CRs during postnatal life is increased in malformations of cortical development (MCDs) and epilepsies.
source: The persistence of CRs during postnatal life is increased in malformations of cortical development (MCDs) and epilepsies thereby opening the intriguing possibility that the maintenance of CRs contributes to the dysfunction of cortical circuits (for review see Luhmann, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Luhmann, 2013

claim: CRs comprise three molecularly distinct subtypes which migrate from different sources that surround the cortical primordium.
source: They comprise three molecularly distinct subtypes which migrate from different sources that surround the cortical primordium: (i) septum and eminentia thalami-derived CRs of the ΔNp73/Dbx1 lineage (SE-CRs); (ii) hem-derived CRs of the ΔNp73/Wnt3a lineage (hem-CRs); (iii) pallial-subpallial boundary-derived CRs of the Dbx1 lineage (PSB-CRs) (Bielle et al., 2005; Yoshida et al., 2006; Tissir et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bielle et al., 2005; Yoshida et al., 2006; Tissir et al., 2009

claim: SE-CRs but not hem-derived CRs die in a Bax-dependent manner.
source: More recently, we showed that subtype-specific differences also exist in their elimination during early postnatal life, with SE- but not hem-derived CRs dying in a Bax-dependent manner, which is a critical player of the apoptotic pathway (Ledonne et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ledonne et al., 2016

claim: CRs express ionotropic glutamatergic and GABAergic receptors and are embedded into immature circuits where they mainly receive GABAergic synaptic inputs.
source: Before their disappearance, CRs express ionotropic glutamatergic and GABAergic receptors and are embedded into immature circuits where they mainly receive GABAergic synaptic inputs, suggesting that these transient cells might have an activity-dependent role in the development of cortical networks (Kirischuk et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kirischuk et al., 2014

claim: CRs density shapes axonal and dendritic outgrowth in LI and impacts onto the excitation/inhibition (E/I) ratio in upper cortical layers.
source: Consistently, we found that CRs density shapes axonal and dendritic outgrowth in LI and impacts onto the excitation/inhibition (E/I) ratio in upper cortical layers (de Frutos et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to de Frutos et al., 2016

claim: Electrical activity was proposed as one of the drivers of CR demise.
source: Conversely, activity was also proposed as one of the drive of CR demise.
evidence: Stated as a proposal in the literature

claim: Studies from Del Rı́o et al. (1996) first highlighted the role played by electrical activity on CR death in vitro.
source: Studies from Del Rı́o et al. (1996) first highlighted the role played by electrical activity on CR death in vitro.
evidence: Supported by citation to Del Rı́o et al., 1996

claim: CRs display electrophysiological features of immature neurons.
source: CRs were shown to display electrophysiological features of immature neurons (Kirischuk et al., 2014; Barber and Pierani, 2016), including the persistent depolarizing action of GABA which was suggested to depend on the maintenance of the chloride inward transporter NKCC1 and the absence of the outward transporter KCC2 (Mienville, 1998; Achilles et al., 2007; Pozas et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kirischuk et al., 2014; Barber and Pierani, 2016; Mienville, 1998; Achilles et al., 2007; Pozas et al., 2008

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of activity and GABA signaling in vitro and global inactivation of NKCC1 in vivo were shown to reduce the death of CRs.
source: Interestingly, pharmacological inhibition of activity and GABA signaling in vitro and global inactivation of NKCC1 in vivo were shown to reduce the death of CRs (Blanquie et al., 2017a; Blanquie et al., 2017b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Blanquie et al., 2017a; Blanquie et al., 2017b

claim: The density of CRs in the somatosensory barrel cortex was unchanged in ΔNp73cre/+;R26Kir2.1/+ animals at postnatal day 7 (P7).
source: We found that the density of CRs in the somatosensory barrel cortex was unchanged in these animals at postnatal day 7 (P7), that is before CRs undergo massive cell death (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A and B

claim: Kir2.1 channel overexpression in ΔNp73-CRs resulted in an increase of CRs with respect to controls in the somatosensory cortex at P15 and P25.
source: In contrast, Kir2.1 channel overexpression in ΔNp73-CRs resulted in an increase of CRs with respect to controls in the somatosensory cortex at P15 and P25 (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A and B

claim: Rescued CRs were hyperpolarized and displayed a decrease in the input resistance without exhibiting changes in action potential properties at both P15 and P25.
source: Importantly, using whole-cell recording, we checked that rescued CRs were, as expected, hyperpolarized and displayed a decrease in the input resistance without exhibiting changes in action potential properties at both P15 and P25 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-C

claim: Most morphological properties were preserved in Kir2.1-expressing CRs, apart from a reduced soma at P25.
source: Biocytin-filling and immunostaining further revealed that most morphological properties were preserved in Kir2.1-expressing CRs, apart from a reduced soma at P25 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by morphological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D

claim: Rescued CRs displayed similar branching length in LI and co-expressed Reelin (Reln) from P7 to P25.
source: In particular, rescued CRs displayed similar branching length in LI (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and E) and co-expressed Reelin (Reln) from P7 to P25 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: Supported by morphological and immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, E, F and G

claim: Hyperpolarization of ΔNp73-CRs does not drastically alter cardinal morphological features of CRs but prevents their complete elimination.
source: Taken together, these experiments show that hyperpolarization of ΔNp73-CRs does not drastically alter cardinal morphological features of CRs but prevents their complete elimination.
evidence: Inferred from the morphological and survival data presented

claim: Hem-CR death was unaffected in Wnt3acre/+;R26Kir2.1/+ mice.
source: We found that hem-CR death was unaffected in this mouse line (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C and D

claim: The proportions of rescued cells in the somatosensory cortex at P25 was evaluated to approximately 30% of the initial pool of ΔNp73-CRs, which corresponds to the expected number of SE-CRs.
source: Moreover, taking into account cortical growth, the proportions of rescued cells in the somatosensory cortex at P25 was evaluated to approximately 30% of the initial pool of ΔNp73-CRs, which corresponds to the expected number of SE-CRs (Bielle et al., 2005; Yoshida et al., 2006; Tissir et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by quantification and citations to Bielle et al., 2005; Yoshida et al., 2006; Tissir et al., 2009

claim: The death of a specific subset of ΔNp73cre/+ SE-CRs is both Bax-dependent and activity-dependent.
source: Collectively, these results show that the death of a specific subset of ΔNp73cre/+ SE-CRs is both Bax-dependent and activity-dependent.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of Bax deletion and Kir2.1 expression experiments

claim: At P9-11 in control ΔNp73cre/+;R26mt/+ mice, sPSCs sensitive to the GABAA receptor (GABAAR) antagonist SR95531 (10 µM) were observed in CRs held at −60 mV.
source: First, at P9-11 in control ΔNp73cre/+;R26mt/+ mice, sPSCs sensitive to the GABAA receptor (GABAAR) antagonist SR95531 (10 µM) were observed in CRs held at −60 mV, confirming that CRs are innervated mainly by functional GABAergic synaptic inputs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B; data not shown for SR95531 application; n = 7).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B

claim: Low-frequency stimulations in LI easily elicited ePSCs that were completely blocked by SR95531 application.
source: Low-frequency stimulations in LI easily elicited ePSCs that were also completely blocked by SR95531 application (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D), even in 0 mM Mg2+ condition, which relieves the Mg2+ block of NMDA receptors.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D

claim: ePSCs were mediated by GABAARs and not by AMPA or NMDA receptors.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that ePSCs were mediated by GABAARs and not by AMPA or NMDA receptors.
evidence: Inferred from the complete blockade by SR95531 even in 0 mM Mg2+ condition

claim: The presence of GABAergic synaptic inputs on CRs was confirmed by immunostainings against the presynaptic marker GAD65/67 and the postsynaptic marker Gephyrin.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Sun et al., 2019), the presence of GABAergic synaptic inputs on CRs was confirmed by immunostainings against the presynaptic marker GAD65/67 and the postsynaptic marker Gephyrin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and citation to Sun et al., 2019

claim: Control GFP+ CRs in ΔNp73cre/+;TauGFP/+ mice expressed very low to undetectable levels of KCC2.
source: In agreement with previous reports (Achilles et al., 2007; Pozas et al., 2008), control GFP+ CRs in ΔNp73cre/+;TauGFP/+ mice expressed very low to undetectable levels of KCC2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and citations to Achilles et al., 2007; Pozas et al., 2008

claim: sPSCs in rescued CRs had similar frequencies, amplitudes and kinetics in both ΔNp73cre/+;R26Kir2.1/+ and ΔNp73cre/+;Baxlox/lox;R26mT/+ models at P23-28.
source: First, we found that sPSCs in rescued CRs had similar frequencies, amplitudes and kinetics in both models (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2A–B

claim: sPSCs in rescued CRs were completely abolished by GABAAR antagonist SR95531, indicating that rescued CRs remained innervated by functional GABAergic synaptic inputs.
source: Moreover, sPSCs were completely abolished by GABAAR antagonist SR95531, indicating that rescued CRs remained innervated by functional GABAergic synaptic inputs (data not shown for SR95531 application, n = 8 and n = 5 for ΔNp73cre/+;R26Kir2.1/+ and ΔNp73cre/+;Baxlox/lox;R26mT/+ mice, respectively).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data

claim: The complete block of ePSCs by SR95531, even in 0 mM Mg2+, revealed that ePSCs were exclusively mediated by GABAARs at hyperpolarized holding potentials in rescued CRs.
source: Consistently, the complete block of ePSCs by SR95531, even in 0 mM Mg2+, revealed that ePSCs were exclusively mediated by GABAARs at hyperpolarized holding potentials, as observed in younger mice (Figure 2C–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2C–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D

claim: A reduced sPSC frequency and ePSC amplitude were observed in rescued CRs compared to P9-P11 mice, suggesting a decreased CR connectivity in the more mature neocortex.
source: While these GABAergic inputs were preserved in rescued CRs, we observed a reduced sPSC frequency and ePSC amplitude compared to P9-P11 mice, suggesting a decreased CR connectivity in the more mature neocortex (Figure 2A–B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2A–B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B

claim: Rescued CRs in both mouse models, in spite of a reduced connectivity compared to earlier stages, are kept integrated in functional neuronal circuits.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that rescued CRs, as previously showed in the early postnatal neocortex (Soda et al., 2003; Sava et al., 2010; Kilb and Luhmann, 2001), receive solely GABAergic synaptic inputs at the time of their death. They further demonstrate that rescued CRs in both mouse models, inspite of a reduced connectivity compared to earlier stages, are kept integrated in functional neuronal circuits.
evidence: Inferred from the electrophysiological data and supported by citations to Soda et al., 2003; Sava et al., 2010; Kilb and Luhmann, 2001

claim: No major changes were observed in the morphology of LII/III pyramidal neurons of ΔNp73cre/+;R26Kir2.1/+ mice compared to their matched controls.
source: While no major changes were observed in the morphology of LII/III pyramidal neurons of ΔNp73cre/+;R26Kir2.1/+ mice compared to their matched controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), major defects were observed for these neurons in ΔNp73cre/+;Baxlox/lox mutants (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by morphological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Major defects were observed in the morphology of LII/III pyramidal neurons in ΔNp73cre/+;Baxlox/lox mutants.
source: While no major changes were observed in the morphology of LII/III pyramidal neurons of ΔNp73cre/+;R26Kir2.1/+ mice compared to their matched controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), major defects were observed for these neurons in ΔNp73cre/+;Baxlox/lox mutants (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by morphological data shown in Figure 3

claim: Quantitative analyses revealed an increase in the number of apical and basal dendritic branches at P25 in ΔNp73cre/+;Baxlox/lox compared to controls.
source: Quantitative analyses revealed an increase in the number of apical and basal dendritic branches at P25 in ΔNp73cre/+;Baxlox/lox compared to controls (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative morphological data shown in Figure 3B

claim: LII/III pyramidal cells displayed an increased complexity for apical dendrites (between 180 µm and 240 µm from the soma) as well as for basal dendrites (between 60 and 80 µm from the soma) in ΔNp73cre/+;Baxlox/lox mutants.
source: We observed that LII/III pyramidal cells displayed an increased complexity for apical dendrites (between 180 µm and 240 µm from the soma) as well as for basal dendrites (between 60 and 80 µm from the soma) (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by Sholl analysis data shown in Figure 3C

claim: No statistically different changes in the number of dendritic branches or the complexity of apical and basal dendrites were detected in LII/LIII pyramidal neurons of the ΔNp73cre/+;R26Kir2.1/+ model.
source: Interestingly, no statistically different changes in the number of dendritic branches (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) or the complexity of apical and basal dendrites (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) were detected in LII/LIII pyramidal neurons of the ΔNp73cre/+;R26Kir2.1/+ model, in which SE-CRs survive but are hyperpolarized.
evidence: Supported by morphological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C

claim: The survival of a specific subset of CRs has a general promoting impact onto the dendritic tree of upper layer pyramidal neurons only when they keep their normal intrinsic excitability.
source: Thus, the survival of a specific subset of CRs has a general promoting impact onto the dendritic tree of upper layer pyramidal neurons only when they keep their normal intrinsic excitability.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of Bax and Kir2.1 mutant phenotypes

claim: SE-CRs survival in LI promotes an exuberance of apical and basal dendrites of LII/LIII pyramidal neurons in an activity-dependent manner.
source: Collectively, our analyses show that SE-CRs survival in LI promotes an exuberance of apical and basal dendrites of LII/LIII pyramidal neurons in an activity-dependent manner.
evidence: Inferred from the combined morphological data from both mutant models

claim: Spine density on both apical and basal dendrites of pyramidal cells was significantly increased in ΔNp73cre/+;Baxlox/lox mutants compared to controls.
source: Spine density on both apical and basal dendrites of pyramidal cells was significantly increased in ΔNp73cre/+;Baxlox/lox mutants compared to controls (Figure 4A and B)
evidence: Supported by spine density quantification data shown in Figure 4A and B

claim: No differences in spine density were observed in ΔNp73cre/+;R26Kir2.1/+ mutants.
source: whereas no differences were observed in ΔNp73cre/+;R26Kir2.1/+ mutants (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Supported by spine density quantification data shown in Figure 4C and D

claim: The survival of electrically-active CRs not only triggers a dendritic exuberance, but also drives an increase in spine densities.
source: These results indicate that the survival of electrically-active CRs not only triggers a dendritic exuberance, but also drives an increase in spine densities.
evidence: Inferred from the combined dendritic and spine density data

claim: Pyramidal cells in ΔNp73cre/+;Baxlox/lox mutants showed a significant increase in the mean amplitude of eEPSCs, while that of eIPSCs remained unchanged compared to controls.
source: Pyramidal cells in ΔNp73cre/+;Baxlox/lox mutants showed a significant increase in the mean amplitude of eEPSCs, while that of eIPSCs remained unchanged compared to controls (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: Pyramidal cells in ΔNp73cre/+;Baxlox/lox mutants showed a significant increase in the E/I ratio.
source: This modification is highlighted by a significant increase in the E/I ratio (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4F

claim: The sEPSC frequency was significantly higher in ΔNp73cre/+;Baxlox/lox mutants with respect to controls while the mean sEPSC amplitude remained unchanged.
source: As expected for an increased number of inputs, the sEPSC frequency was significantly higher in ΔNp73cre/+;Baxlox/lox mutants with respect to controls while the mean sEPSC amplitude remained unchanged (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D

claim: No differences were observed in the amplitudes of both eEPSCs and eIPSCs or in the E/I ratio in ΔNp73cre/+;R26Kir2.1/+ mutants.
source: When the same experiments were performed in ΔNp73cre/+;R26Kir2.1/+ mutants, no differences were observed either in the amplitudes of both eEPSCs and eIPSCs or in the E/I ratio (Figure 4G–H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4G–H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: Changes were neither observed in the frequency of sEPSCs of ΔNp73cre/+;R26Kir2.1/+ mutants, showing that defects in the synaptic activity of pyramidal neurons is dependent on the intrinsic activity of rescued CRs.
source: In line with this, changes were neither observed in the frequency of sEPSCs of these mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), showing that defects in the synaptic activity of pyramidal neurons is dependent on the intrinsic activity of rescued CRs.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E

claim: Light-evoked responses could not be detected during patch-clamp or extracellular recordings of Layer I interneurons or LFPs, even in the presence of 0 mM Mg2+, 3 mM Ca2+ and 50 µM of the potassium channel blocker 4AP.
source: We could never detect light-evoked responses during patch-clamp or extracellular recordings, even in the presence of 0 mM Mg2+, 3 mM Ca2+ and 50 µM of the potassium channel blocker 4AP, a treatment that renders all neurons more excitable (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic and electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G

claim: The low proportion of rescued CRs compared to pyramidal neurons and the lack of electrical extracellular responses during their sustained light stimulation suggest that direct synaptic inputs from CRs cannot account for the robust morphological and functional changes induced in pyramidal cells by the aberrant CR survival.
source: Although these results do not rule out that rescued CRs contact other neurons through bona fide glutamatergic synapses, the low proportion of these cells compared to pyramidal neurons and the lack of electrical extracellular responses during their sustained light stimulation suggest that direct synaptic inputs from CRs cannot account for the robust morphological and functional changes induced in pyramidal cells by the aberrant CR survival.
evidence: Inferred from the optogenetic and electrophysiological data

claim: The survival of electrically-active SE-CRs increases the excitatory inputs to upper pyramidal neurons, possibly through a non-glutamatergic mechanism, thereby generating a E/I imbalance and functional changes in circuit wiring.
source: Overall, these experiments show that the survival of electrically-active SE-CRs increases the excitatory inputs to upper pyramidal neurons, possibly through a non-glutamatergic mechanism, thereby generating a E/I imbalance and functional changes in circuit wiring.
evidence: Inferred from the combined electrophysiological and optogenetic data

claim: The elimination of specific subsets of CRs, SE-CRs, is activity-dependent and this process is essential for proper cortical wiring.
source: Our results show that the elimination of specific subsets of CRs, SE-CRs, is activity-dependent and that this process is essential for proper cortical wiring.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of the study

claim: The persistence of SE-CRs beyond their normal phase of elimination triggered major deficits in LII/LIII somatosensory pyramidal neurons.
source: Indeed, the persistence of SE-CRs beyond their normal phase of elimination triggered major deficits in LII/LIII somatosensory pyramidal neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the morphological and electrophysiological data

claim: The analyzed neurons displayed an increased dendritic arborization and spine density, and consistently showed enhanced excitatory inputs leading to a functional E/I imbalance.
source: Not only the analyzed neurons displayed an increased dendritic arborization and spine density, but they also consistently showed enhanced excitatory inputs leading to a functional E/I imbalance.
evidence: Inferred from the morphological and electrophysiological data

claim: These anatomical and electrophysiological deficits all relied on the fact that persistent CRs were electrically-active.
source: Remarkably, these anatomical and electrophysiological deficits all relied on the fact that persistent CRs were electrically-active.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of Bax and Kir2.1 mutant phenotypes

claim: Activity is required to eliminate SE-CRs, whose survival would otherwise perturb cortical wiring in an activity-dependent manner.
source: Our study thus demonstrates that activity is required to eliminate SE-CRs, whose survival would otherwise perturb cortical wiring in an activity-dependent manner.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of the study

claim: The study reveals an elegant interplay between transient CRs and neuronal activity in the construction of functional cortical excitatory circuits.
source: Taken together, it reveals an elegant interplay between transient CRs and neuronal activity in the construction of functional cortical excitatory circuits.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of the study

claim: Activity was reported to promote survival of both glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons in the neocortex and in general in the nervous system.
source: Activity was reported to promote survival of both glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons in the neocortex and in general in the nervous system ( Blanquie et al., 2017a; Causeret et al., 2018; Wong and Marín, 2019), providing a mean to integrate around 70% of neurons into functional circuits.
evidence: Supported by citations to Blanquie et al., 2017a; Causeret et al., 2018; Wong and Marín, 2019

claim: CRs display 'immature' features such as a depolarized resting potential and a very high input resistance.
source: These neurons display 'immature' features such as a depolarized resting potential and a very high input resistance (Kirischuk et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kirischuk et al., 2014

claim: GABA is depolarizing in CRs due to their elevated intracellular chloride concentration resulting from the activity of the chloride inward transporter NKCC1 in the absence of expression of chloride outward transporter KCC2.
source: Especially, GABA is depolarizing in these cells due to their elevated intracellular chloride concentration resulting from the activity of the chloride inward transporter NKCC1 in the absence of expression of chloride outward transporter KCC2 (Mienville, 1998; Achilles et al., 2007; Pozas et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mienville, 1998; Achilles et al., 2007; Pozas et al., 2008

claim: The pharmacological blockade of NKCC1 in cell cultures or the genetic ablation of this transporter in vivo promotes the survival of a CR population, probably by preventing GABAA receptor-mediated depolarization.
source: Interestingly, the pharmacological blockade of NKCC1 in cell cultures or the genetic ablation of this transporter in vivo promotes the survival of a CR population, probably by preventing GABAA receptor-mediated depolarization (Blanquie et al., 2017b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Blanquie et al., 2017b

claim: The depolarizing effect of GABA will depend most probably on the levels of neuronal activity since high activity levels attenuate the GABAA receptor-mediated excitatory drive in CRs.
source: It must be considered, however, that the depolarizing effect of GABA will depend most probably on the levels of neuronal activity since high activity levels attenuate the GABAA receptor-mediated excitatory drive in CRs (Kolbaev et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kolbaev et al., 2011

claim: CRs receive GABAergic synaptic inputs from different sources, including local interneurons of Layer I, the underlying layers of the neocortex and the subplate, as well as the zona incerta.
source: CRs receive GABAergic synaptic inputs from different sources, including local interneurons of Layer I, the underlying layers of the neocortex and the subplate, a transient cortical structure absent in the fourth postnatal week, as well as the zona incerta (Kirmse et al., 2007; Myakhar et al., 2011; Kirischuk et al., 2014; Chen and Kriegstein, 2015; Sun et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kirmse et al., 2007; Myakhar et al., 2011; Kirischuk et al., 2014; Chen and Kriegstein, 2015; Sun et al., 2019

claim: Rescued CRs in Layer I might lose GABAergic innervation from transient or distant populations (i.e. subplate and zona incerta) during maturation of neuronal networks, restricting their connectivity with more local neocortical inputs.
source: One interesting possibility is that rescued CRs in Layer I might lose GABAergic innervation from transient or distant populations (i.e. subplate and zona incerta) during maturation of neuronal networks, restricting their connectivity with more local neocortical inputs.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the reduced connectivity observed

claim: A plausible explanation is that GABAergic inputs cannot exert their depolarizing effect as in normal conditions in Kir2.1-expressing CRs, thereby preventing cell death.
source: Since CRs are highly hyperpolarized in this mouse model, a plausible explanation is that GABAergic inputs cannot exert their depolarizing effect as in normal conditions, thereby preventing cell death.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the mechanism of CR survival

claim: Neuronal activity via intracellular calcium signals could trigger apoptosis, as reported during excitotoxicity.
source: In this context, it is also tempting to hypothesize that, as shown in other systems, neuronal activity via intracellular calcium signals could trigger apoptosis, as reported during excitotoxicity (Blanquie et al., 2017a).
evidence: Speculative hypothesis supported by citation to Blanquie et al., 2017a

claim: The timing of SE-CRs death, namely the second postnatal week, corresponds to a major switch in cortical activity and in GABAergic circuits.
source: The timing of SE-CRs death, namely the second postnatal week, corresponds to a major switch in cortical activity (Luhmann and Khazipov, 2018) and in GABAergic circuits (Cossart, 2011), raising the possibility that the elimination of CRs is part of a more global activity-dependent remodeling of cortical circuits.
evidence: Supported by citations to Luhmann and Khazipov, 2018 and Cossart, 2011

claim: Hem-derived CRs die in a Bax- and activity-independent manner, in contrast to SE-CRs that survive in Bax and Kir2.1 mutants.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that hem-derived CRs die in a Bax- and activity-independent manner, in contrast to SE-CRs that survive in Bax and Kir2.1 mutants.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of the study

claim: Hippocampal CRs, which mostly derive from the cortical hem, display a delayed death which seems to occur independently of the apoptotic-specific Caspase-3 activity.
source: Interestingly, hippocampal CRs, which mostly derive from the cortical hem (Louvi et al., 2007) display a delayed death which seems to occur independently of the apoptotic-specific Caspase-3 activity (Anstötz et al., 2016; Anstötz et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Louvi et al., 2007; Anstötz et al., 2016; Anstötz et al., 2018

claim: CR subtypes are intrinsically different in the mechanism determining their demise and argues in favor of complex yet unappreciated subtype-specific pathways leading ultimately to cell death.
source: Together, these data support the notion that CR subtypes are intrinsically different in the mechanism determining their demise and argues in favor of complex yet unappreciated subtype-specific pathways leading ultimately to cell death.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of the study and literature

claim: The effect on basal dendrites might be circuit-mediated since excitatory entries in apical dendritic tufts were shown to modify basal dendrite synaptic plasticity.
source: While the effect on apical dendrites could be direct via local surviving SE-CRs, the impact on basal ones might be circuit-mediated since excitatory entries in apical dendritic tufts were shown to modify basal dendrite synaptic plasticity (Williams and Holtmaat, 2019).
evidence: Speculative explanation supported by citation to Williams and Holtmaat, 2019

claim: Aberrant reduction of CRs during development triggers decreased apical dendritic tufts and dendritic spine density of LII/III pyramidal neurons accompanied by a reduction in the E/I ratio.
source: Conversely, recent work showed that aberrant reduction of CRs during development triggers decreased apical dendritic tufts and dendritic spine density of LII/III pyramidal neurons accompanied by a reduction in the E/I ratio (de Frutos et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to de Frutos et al., 2016

claim: The proper balance of CRs constitutes an essential, yet underappreciated, regulator of LII/III pyramidal neuron morphology and wiring.
source: Taken together our findings reveal that the proper balance of CRs constitutes an essential, yet underappreciated, regulator of LII/III pyramidal neuron morphology and wiring.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of the study and literature

claim: The impact of reducing CR density on LII/III apical dendrites does not rely exclusively on the intrinsic excitability of CRs.
source: Indeed, Kir2.1 expressing mice appear largely similar to controls, suggesting that the impact of reducing CR density on LII/III apical dendrites (de Frutos et al., 2016) does not rely exclusively on the intrinsic excitability of CRs.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of Kir2.1 mutant phenotype with previous work, supported by citation to de Frutos et al., 2016

claim: The lack of response observed during optogenetic experiments suggest that morphological and functional changes may not depend on a direct CR excitatory synaptic input onto principal neurons.
source: The lack of response observed during our optogenetic experiments suggest that these changes may not depend on a direct CR excitatory synaptic input onto principal neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the optogenetic data

claim: Only very few pyramidal cells could be detected as an output of CR cells in the hippocampus during the third postnatal week.
source: This is in line with recent data obtained with experiments performed in the hippocampus using ChR2 activation and paired-recordings in the third postnatal week, where CRs are still present in high density (Quattrocolo and Maccaferri, 2014; Anstötz et al., 2016). Indeed, only very few pyramidal cells could be detected as an output of CR cells.
evidence: Supported by citations to Quattrocolo and Maccaferri, 2014; Anstötz et al., 2016

claim: Excitatory entries onto apical dendrites are emerging as major actors in sensory gating, cortical integration and reward.
source: Regardless the mechanism and since excitatory entries onto apical dendrites are emerging as major actors in sensory gating, cortical integration and reward (Keller and Mrsic-Flogel, 2018; Khan and Hofer, 2018; Lacefield et al., 2019; Williams and Holtmaat, 2019; Zhang and Bruno, 2019), our findings highlight the importance of a transient cell population in the emergence of functional circuits as well as the deleterious effects of their abnormal demise.
evidence: Supported by citations to Keller and Mrsic-Flogel, 2018; Khan and Hofer, 2018; Lacefield et al., 2019; Williams and Holtmaat, 2019; Zhang and Bruno, 2019

claim: The elimination of SE-CRs in the somatosensory cortex is required for proper morphology and wiring of LII/III pyramidal neurons.
source: Our study thus shows that the elimination of SE-CRs in the somatosensory cortex is required for proper morphology and wiring of LII/III pyramidal neurons and reveals a remarkable interplay between activity, the elimination of transient cells and cortical wiring.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of the study

claim: Activity, likely driven by cortical maturation, regulates the elimination of transient CRs that would otherwise perturb upper layer wiring.
source: Indeed, activity, likely driven by cortical maturation, regulates the elimination of transient CRs that would otherwise perturb upper layer wiring.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of the study

source: Notably, CRs persistence has been described in human pathological conditions, often associated with epilepsy.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: The work provides novel insights onto normal wiring of upper layers and addresses the functional consequences of incomplete CR removal with major relevance for neurodevelopmental diseases, such as autism spectrum disorder, schizophrenia or epilepsy.
source: Our work thus not only provides novel insights onto normal wiring of upper layers, but also addresses the functional consequences of incomplete CR removal with major relevance for neurodevelopmental diseases, such as autism spectrum disorder, schizophrenia or epilepsy.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of the study and their implications

claim: The ΔNp73cre/+ mouse line targets approximately 80% of CRs, namely hem-CRs (Wnt3a lineage) and SE-CRs.
source: The ΔNp73cre/+ mouse line targets approximately 80% of CRs, namely hem-CRs (Wnt3a lineage) and SE-CRs (Tissir et al., 2009; Griveau et al., 2010; Yoshida et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tissir et al., 2009; Griveau et al., 2010; Yoshida et al., 2006

claim: Wnt3a-derived hem-CRs correspond to about 70% of the ΔNp73-CRs at early postnatal stages.
source: Since hem-CRs are not eliminated via a Bax-dependent process (Ledonne et al., 2016), we investigated whether their survival is sensitive to hyperpolarization. We thus overexpressed Kir2.1 specifically in hem-CRs using the Wnt3acre/+, which corresponds to about 70% of the ΔNp73-CRs at early postnatal stages (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ledonne et al., 2016 and data shown in Figure 1C and D

claim: In ΔNp73cre/+;Baxlox/lox;R26mT/+ mice, a five-fold increase in CR numbers, corresponding to approximately 30% of the initial pool at P7, is detected.
source: Indeed, in both deletion of Bax (Ledonne et al., 2016) or over-expression of Kir2.1 (this manuscript) models, a five-fold increase in CR numbers, corresponding to approximately 30% of the initial pool at P7, is detected when using the ΔNp73Cre line, in contrast to none when using the hem-specific Wnt3aCre line.
evidence: Supported by quantification data and citation to Ledonne et al., 2016

claim: The 30% of rescued CRs in ΔNp73Cre corresponds to a large fraction, if not all, of the SE-CR population.
source: Since hem-CRs constitute about 70% of the population targeted by the ΔNp73Cre line (Bielle et al., 2005; Yoshida et al., 2006; Tissir et al., 2009), our findings support that the 30% of rescued CRs in ΔNp73Cre corresponds to a large fraction, if not all, of the SE-CR population.
evidence: Inferred from quantification data and supported by citations to Bielle et al., 2005; Yoshida et al., 2006; Tissir et al., 2009
